entries.exodus 8:17: Aaron does it, and the dust turns into insects on people and animals everywhere. The reader sees that God's power affects all of creation, not just humans.
entries.exodus 8:18: The magicians try to make insects but cannot, even though the insects are on everyone. The reader sees a clear limit to human power compared with God's.
entries.exodus 8:19: The magicians tell Pharaoh this is God's doing, but Pharaoh still refuses to listen. The reader sees that even clear evidence can be ignored by a stubborn heart.
entries.exodus 8:20: God tells Moses to meet Pharaoh early by the water and repeat the demand to let the people go. The reader sees God giving Pharaoh another chance to obey.
entries.exodus 8:21: If Pharaoh refuses, God will send swarms of flies on him, his officials, his people and their houses. The reader sees the warning is specific and serious.
entries.exodus 8:22: God will keep the flies out of Goshen where his people live, so Pharaoh will know the Lord is over all the earth. The reader sees God protecting his own people while judging others.
entries.exodus 8:23: God will make a clear difference between his people and Pharaoh's people, and the sign will come tomorrow. The reader sees God's timing is set and certain.
entries.exodus 8:24: The flies come and fill Pharaoh's house and the whole land, ruining it. The reader sees that God's warning was not empty.
entries.exodus 8:25: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron and offers a compromise: worship God here in Egypt. The reader sees that partial obedience is often offered instead of full obedience.
entries.exodus 8:26: Moses says that would not be right, because the Israelites' sacrifices would offend the Egyptians and could get them killed. The reader sees Moses refusing a plan that would cause real danger and disrespect.
entries.exodus 8:27: Moses insists they must travel three days into the desert to worship as God commands. The reader sees that God's instructions are not negotiable.
entries.exodus 8:28: Pharaoh agrees to let them go into the desert but not far, and asks Moses to pray for him. The reader sees Pharaoh still trying to control the terms.
entries.exodus 8:29: Moses promises to pray for the flies to leave tomorrow and warns Pharaoh not to deceive them again. The reader sees Moses holding Pharaoh accountable while still willing to pray for him.
entries.exodus 8:30: Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to the Lord. The reader sees faithful prayer even after a tense negotiation.
entries.exodus 8:31: The Lord answers and removes all the flies, not one left. The reader sees God's complete deliverance in response to prayer.
entries.exodus 8:32: But Pharaoh hardens his heart again and does not let the people go. The reader sees that repeated refusal makes a person more set in their ways.
entries.exodus 9:1: God tells Moses to go to Pharaoh and demand that he let the Israelites go so they can worship God. It shows God gives Pharaoh a clear chance to obey before judgment comes.
entries.exodus 9:2: God warns that if Pharaoh keeps refusing to release the people, there will be consequences. Refusing God's clear command brings trouble, not safety.
entries.exodus 9:3: God says a terrible disease will strike Egypt's livestock—horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. The things people depend on for work and wealth are not beyond God's reach.
entries.exodus 9:4: God will spare the Israelites' animals while Egypt's animals die, showing He makes a clear difference between His people and those who oppose Him. God protects His own even in the middle of judgment.
entries.exodus 9:5: God sets an exact time for this to happen: tomorrow. God's warnings are not vague threats; He keeps His word on schedule.
entries.exodus 9:6: The next day it happens just as God said—all Egypt's livestock die, but none of Israel's animals are lost. God's word proves completely reliable.
entries.exodus 9:7: Pharaoh checks and finds Israel's animals untouched, yet he still refuses to let the people go. Seeing God's protection should soften a heart, but pride can keep someone stubborn.
entries.exodus 9:8: God tells Moses and Aaron to take handfuls of soot from a furnace and have Moses throw it into the air in front of Pharaoh. This sets up the next sign in a visible, simple way.
entries.exodus 9:9: The dust will spread over Egypt and cause painful boils on people and animals everywhere. God's judgment reaches even the bodies of those who defy Him.
entries.exodus 9:10: They do exactly as God said, and boils break out on people and animals all over Egypt. Obeying God's instructions brings about exactly what He promised.
entries.exodus 9:11: Egypt's magicians can't even stand before Moses because they are covered in boils too. The powers people trust in fail when God acts.
entries.exodus 9:12: God hardens Pharaoh's heart, and he refuses to listen, just as God had said. Persistent refusal of God can lead to a heart that no longer responds.
entries.exodus 9:13: God again sends Moses early in the morning to demand that Pharaoh release the people to worship Him. God keeps giving Pharaoh opportunities to obey, even after many refusals.
entries.exodus 9:14: This time God will bring the full force of His judgments on Pharaoh, his officials, and his people, so everyone will know no one is like Him. God acts so that people will recognize who He truly is.
entries.exodus 9:15: God says He could have wiped Pharaoh and his people off the earth already. The fact that they are still alive is mercy, not weakness.
entries.exodus 9:16: God let Pharaoh survive to show His power and make His name known everywhere. Even a stubborn ruler serves God's purpose of displaying who God is.
entries.exodus 9:17: God asks Pharaoh why he is still proud and refuses to let the people go. Pride is the root of Pharaoh's stubbornness, and God confronts it directly.
entries.exodus 9:18: God announces that tomorrow He will send the worst hailstorm Egypt has ever seen. The warning gives people time to act and shows God's judgment is coming.
entries.exodus 9:19: God tells Pharaoh to bring his livestock and workers in from the fields, because anything left outside will be killed by the hail. God's warning is also an invitation to take shelter and be spared.
entries.exodus 9:20: Some of Pharaoh's officials fear God's word and quickly bring their servants and animals indoors. Taking God's warnings seriously saves people from harm.
entries.exodus 9:21: Those who ignore God's warning leave their servants and animals out in the fields. Disregarding God's word puts people and what they care about in danger.
entries.exodus 9:22: God tells Moses to stretch out his hand so hail will fall on all Egypt—on people, animals, and plants. God's judgment covers the whole land, not just part of it.
entries.exodus 9:23: Moses raises his staff, and God sends thunder, hail, and fire running along the ground. God's word through Moses brings immediate and powerful results.
entries.exodus 9:24: The hail is mixed with fire and is more severe than anything Egypt has seen since it became a nation. This is an unprecedented judgment, showing the seriousness of resisting God.
entries.exodus 9:25: The hail strikes everything left in the fields—people, animals, plants, and trees—across Egypt. Nothing exposed is safe when God's judgment falls.
entries.exodus 9:26: Only in Goshen, where the Israelites live, is there no hail. God again makes a clear distinction, protecting His people while judging Egypt.
entries.exodus 9:27: Pharaoh admits he has sinned and that God is right while he and his people are wrong. Even a hard heart can momentarily acknowledge the truth under pressure.
entries.exodus 9:28: Pharaoh begs Moses to pray for the thunder and hail to stop and promises to let the people go. Fear of suffering can produce promises that don't last.
entries.exodus 9:29: Moses says he will pray outside the city, and the storm will stop so Pharaoh will know the earth belongs to the Lord. God's power over nature is meant to show He rules over all.
entries.exodus 9:30: Moses tells Pharaoh plainly that he and his officials still don't truly fear God. Words of repentance can be empty if the heart hasn't changed.
entries.exodus 9:31: The flax and barley were destroyed because the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom. The judgment hits real crops at a real season, causing real loss.
entries.exodus 9:32: The wheat and spelt were spared because they grow later and hadn't come up yet. Even in judgment, God's timing leaves some things untouched.
entries.exodus 9:33: Moses leaves the city, prays to God, and the thunder, hail, and rain stop. God answers prayer and shows His control over the storm.
entries.exodus 9:34: Once the storm stops, Pharaoh sins again and hardens his heart along with his officials. Relief from trouble doesn't automatically change a stubborn heart.
entries.exodus 9:35: Pharaoh's heart stays hard and he refuses to let the people go, just as God had said through Moses. God's word proves true even when people refuse to change.
entries.exodus 10:1: God tells Moses to go back to Pharaoh, because God himself has made Pharaoh and his officials stubborn. This means God is using Pharaoh's resistance to display his power openly.
entries.exodus 10:2: God wants the story of his miracles in Egypt passed down from parents to children and grandchildren. For the reader, it means remembering and telling what God has done keeps faith alive across generations.
entries.exodus 10:3: Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh with God's question: how long will you stay proud and refuse to let my people go to worship me? It means pride that resists God only brings trouble.
entries.exodus 10:4: God warns that refusing to release the people will bring a plague of locusts the very next day. It shows that ignoring God's warning has real consequences.
entries.exodus 10:5: The locusts will be so thick they cover the ground and eat every plant and tree left after the earlier hail. It means the coming judgment will be total, leaving nothing spared.
entries.exodus 10:6: The locusts will fill the houses of Pharaoh, his officials, and all Egypt, worse than anything their ancestors ever saw. It means this disaster will be unlike anything in living memory.
entries.exodus 10:7: Pharaoh's own officials urge him to let the men go, asking how long he will keep causing ruin and whether he sees Egypt is being destroyed. It means even those around a stubborn leader can see the damage being done.
entries.exodus 10:8: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron back and agrees to let the people worship, but asks who exactly will go. It shows he is still trying to control the terms rather than fully obey.
entries.exodus 10:9: Moses answers that everyone will go—young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds—because they are holding a festival to the Lord. It means wholehearted worship gives God everything, not just a part.
entries.exodus 10:10: Pharaoh sarcastically says he will let them and their children go only if the Lord helps them, accusing them of evil intent. It means he is mocking their request and still refusing to truly release them.
entries.exodus 10:11: Pharaoh refuses to let the women and children go, allowing only the men, and drives Moses and Aaron out. It means he wants to keep leverage over the people so they must return.
entries.exodus 10:12: God tells Moses to stretch out his hand so locusts will come and eat every green plant left in Egypt. It means God is about to carry out the warning he gave.
entries.exodus 10:13: Moses raises his staff, and God sends an east wind all day and night that brings the locusts in the morning. It shows God directing even the wind to accomplish his purpose.
entries.exodus 10:14: The locusts swarm over the whole land in numbers never seen before or since. It means this plague is unprecedented in its scale.
entries.exodus 10:15: The locusts cover the ground until it looks black and eat every green plant and fruit left after the hail. It means nothing green remains anywhere in Egypt.
entries.exodus 10:16: Pharaoh quickly calls for Moses and Aaron and admits he has sinned against the Lord and against them. It means even a hard heart can be forced to confess wrongdoing under pressure.
entries.exodus 10:17: Pharaoh asks forgiveness just this once and begs Moses to pray that this deadly plague be removed. It means his repentance is shallow and focused only on relief from suffering.
entries.exodus 10:18: Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to the Lord. It shows Moses faithfully interceding even for the one who oppresses his people.
entries.exodus 10:19: God sends a strong west wind that carries the locusts into the Red Sea, leaving none in Egypt. It means God completely reverses the disaster in response to prayer.
entries.exodus 10:20: But God makes Pharaoh's heart hard again, and he refuses to let the Israelites go. It means relief from judgment does not change a heart that will not truly submit.
entries.exodus 10:21: God tells Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven so that darkness falls over Egypt, thick enough that people grope around. It means the next judgment will be a terrifying loss of light.
entries.exodus 10:22: Moses stretches out his hand, and deep darkness covers all Egypt for three days. It means the land is plunged into total, unnatural darkness.
entries.exodus 10:23: People cannot see each other or leave their places for three days, but the Israelites have light where they live. It means God protects and distinguishes his people even in the middle of judgment.
entries.exodus 10:24: Pharaoh calls Moses and offers to let the people worship, but insists their flocks and herds stay behind, with the children allowed to go. It means he is still bargaining and holding back what God requires.
entries.exodus 10:25: Moses replies that Pharaoh must also provide animals for burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord. It means worship requires giving God what he asks, not just what is convenient.
entries.exodus 10:26: Moses insists all their livestock must go, not one left behind, because they need them for worship and don't yet know what offerings to give. It means complete obedience leaves nothing held back from God.
entries.exodus 10:27: But God makes Pharaoh's heart hard, and he refuses to let the people go. It means the cycle of stubbornness continues despite every warning.
entries.exodus 10:28: Pharaoh angrily tells Moses to leave and warns that seeing his face again will mean death. It means the relationship between Pharaoh and Moses is now completely broken.
entries.exodus 10:29: Moses agrees, saying he will never see Pharaoh's face again. It means the final break has come, and the next encounter will bring the last judgment.
